findings.title: Favor and harm disclose a formed response
findings.claim: When favor is bestowed, the generic human turns away and draws his side back; when harm reaches him, hope collapses. The next verse relates each person's action to their own shakilah, so the paired reactions can be read as responses that disclose an orientation.
findings.mechanism: The focus pairs bestowed benefit with aversive turning and harmful contact with despair. At 17:84, each person's action is tied to that person's shakilah and God knows who is more guided on a path. This contact changes a list of fickle reactions into actions that express a formed response, while the focus conditions remain their immediate occasions.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the body's withdrawal and the collapse of hope as two different expressions of how a person receives circumstances.
findings.containment: The focus still states conditional human responses. The following verse supplies an interpretive frame; it does not establish that every person always reacts this way or identify the unspoken object of aversion.

epistemic.reason: The trusted pericope nomination is anchored in exact focus branches, and the supplied 17:84 connection is reassessed against its exact Arabic.

findings.claim: The focus's mild-contact wording meets its abrupt despair, while 17:82 places healing and mercy beside an increase in loss for different recipients and 17:84 ties action to each person's shakilah. The focus can therefore be read as a disposition-mediated amplification of response.
findings.mechanism: The focus pairs bestowed favor with turning away and harm touching the person with despair. The preceding verse says the Qur'an is healing and mercy for believers but increases loss for wrongdoers; the next relates each act to a shakilah. The focus verb for bestowal also has a registered increase facet, activated by 17:82's separate increase verb. Together, these contacts make reception the link between circumstance and outcome.
findings.reader_payoff: The result is not read as a simple measure of input size: the same surrounding discourse permits benefit, loss, and sharply different responses, while the focus's own bestowal verb meets an explicit increase-in-loss image.
findings.containment: 17:82 specifically speaks of the Qur'an and named recipient groups; the focus does not identify its bestowed favor with that discourse. The increase facet colors the focus verb without replacing its ordinary benefaction sense, and the receiver-disposition link remains a qualified contextual analogy.

epistemic.reason: All HFT word/root coordinates align with the lean context projections, and the two adjacent verses supply exact Arabic contact; the reader identity is legacy_unbound and the comparison remains inferential.

findings.claim: The focus's bestowed favor and withdrawal meet the following verses' conditional removal of what was revealed, the absence of any keeper, and the naming of mercy and great favor. Read together, this gives the focus an attributed image of treating a gift as secure until its dependence becomes visible.
findings.mechanism: The focus names benefit delivered and a recipient who turns away; 17:86 states that what was revealed could be taken and no keeper could secure it, while 17:87 calls its continuation mercy and great favor. That contact changes the focus from a simple report of ungrateful response into a bounded reflection on false custody and dependence.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees withdrawal occurring while favor is present against a sequence that makes continued possession contingent and unprotected by any independent keeper.
findings.containment: 17:86 specifically names the revealed message, not every favor in 17:83. The focus does not say the person consciously claims ownership; false self-custody is the HFT's qualified inference.

epistemic.reason: The trace coordinates match the supplied 17:86-87 surfaces and roots, but the record is legacy_unbound and its extension from the revealed message to the focus favor is explicitly limited.

findings.claim: The focus's distancing and bodily flank can be heard through a rain-deflecting boundary image; the later demands for springs, rivers, and channels add a separate image of beneficial flow on specified terms, while harm still reaches the person.
findings.mechanism: The registered rain-barrier facet of the focus root and the side-shield branch meet the exact water-demand surfaces of 17:90-91; the focus's harmful-contact verb supplies penetration of the boundary. This contact lets the sequence be modeled as control of what enters and where beneficial flow should emerge.
findings.reader_payoff: The focus withdrawal and later water demands become a single material analogy about guarding an edge while asking for life-giving flow, with harmful contact marking the limit of that control.
findings.containment: This is an exploratory material analogy, not the lexical translation of the focus verb or flank. The later speakers' requests remain their stated demands; no intent to build a water-control system is asserted.

epistemic.reason: The exact focus/context surfaces and all cited indices align, but the HFT identity is legacy_unbound and the rain-barrier-to-water sequence is an expressly surprising analogy.

findings.title: A human-facing side turned away
findings.claim: The focus keeps its ordinary human and bodily-flank meanings, while an attributed root-image relation lets the registered human-facing-side branch meet the flank that is carried away. The next supplied verses place the human kind against jinn and then show refusal, leaving a bounded inversion of relational orientation visible.
findings.mechanism: The focus human noun is the attributed carrier for the human-facing-side image; the independent sideward-distance verb and explicit flank make a turning-away contact. At 17:88 the human-kind term is directly contrasted with jinn, while the correctly aligned refusal word at 17:89 supplies a later collective response. The relation changes a generic human subject into a spatially oriented participant without changing the noun's ordinary gloss.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the focus's bodily turn as an inversion of a human-oriented relation, then see the following human/jinn contrast and refusal keep the ordinary human-kind reading present.
findings.containment: This is the HFT's exploratory branchplay, not an etymology of الإنسان: the registered branch excludes human itself as its lexical gloss. The 17:89 people occurrences are not routed through this root because the supplied projection gives ن و س, not ء ن س; 17:89 contributes only through its separately aligned refusal occurrence.

epistemic.reason: The focus coordinate/root and 17:88 human occurrence match the trace, but the branch boundary requires a relational analogy rather than a lexical gloss, and the 17:89 الناس root assignment in the HFT trace conflicts with the packet.

findings.title: The favored path gives another reception to the gift
findings.claim: Under the explicitly supplied Fātiḥa overlay, the focus's bestowed favor and subsequent turning can be read beside the path of those You favored. The repeated bestowal phrase gives a distinct positive reception alongside the focus's withdrawal.
findings.mechanism: The focus says that favor is bestowed upon the human before he turns away. In 1:7, the same bestowal verb and recipient construction occurs inside the path of those favored, after 1:6 asks for guidance to the straight path. The shared wording contacts the external path frame and changes the focus response into one possible reception of favor beside a path whose recipients remain oriented toward guidance.
findings.reader_payoff: Favor now has two supplied receptions in this selected recitation: the focus's turning aside and the Fātiḥa's path of those favored.
findings.containment: The external verses do not identify the focus's generic human with the Fātiḥa's recipients or say that the focus favor is guidance. The contact is the repeated bestowal construction under the declared overlay.

epistemic.reason: The repeated bestowal construction and path wording are present in the supplied focus and external surfaces; the comparison is a bounded authorial inference, not an identity claim.
